# Output Table
## First Step
The function will first need to calculate whether the author actually quit. We can do that by calculating the elapsed time between now (the current time) and the last commit message of the author. The inactivity threshold is greater than 3 months, so around 90 days at the minimum. The function will contain a parameter titled `quit_lag` which defines an integer in days, with a default set to 90 days. The function will take in `timestamp` and subtract it from the current time. If the result is greater than `quit_lag` then we can return `True` (the author did quit) and we will save the date they quit as a column, which we'll call `quit_date`. Otherwise we return `False` (the author did not quit).

## Second Step
Now, we will need to see whether the developer raged. We will be working based on the author's last commit message. The function will be checking the `message` input against the `sentiment_value` input. If, in the data table, Alice's message has an assigned sentiment value of `-1`, then we can say `True` (Alice did rage). Otherwise if the sentiment value is `0`, or `1` then we can say `False` (Alice did not rage). We can do these checks against all of the author's last commit message in the input table.

## Third Step
Now that we have computed whether the author quit and whether the author raged, we can see whether the author both quit AND raged. From our First Step and Second Step, if the result was 1) `True`, the author did quit, and 2) `True`, the author did rage, then we can say 3) `True`, the author did ragequit. Otherwise if either the first or second steps was `False`, then we can say `False`, the author did not ragequit.

The resulting output table would look something like the following:
| author | quit  | quit_date           | rage  | ragequit |
|--------|-------|--------------------|-------|----------|
| Alice (alice@email.com)  | FALSE | NA                 | TRUE  | FALSE    |
| Bob (bob@email.com) | TRUE  | 2024-06-10 16:45:00 | FALSE | FALSE    |

| David (david@email.com) | FALSE | NA                 | FALSE | FALSE    |
| Elena (elena@email.com)  | TRUE  | 2025-07-12 17:30:00 | FALSE | FALSE    |

```r
transform_dependencies_to_network <- function(depends_parsed, weight_types=NA){
  src <- dest <- weight <- NULL # due to NSE notes in R CMD check
  # Can only include types user wants if Depends found them at least once on codebase

  nodes <- depends_parsed[["nodes"]]
  edgelist <- depends_parsed[["edgelist"]]

  # Capture NA intent before intersect converts it to character(0)
  use_all_types <- any(is.na(weight_types))
  weight_types <- intersect(names(edgelist)[3:ncol(edgelist)], weight_types)

  # copy() preserves all dependency type columns and prevents data.table
  # reference mutation of the caller's depends_parsed object
  dependency_edgelist <- copy(edgelist)

  if(use_all_types){
    dependency_edgelist$weight <- rowSums(edgelist[,3:ncol(edgelist),with=FALSE])
  }else{
    dependency_edgelist$weight <- rowSums(edgelist[,weight_types,with=FALSE])
  }

  # Remove dependencies not chosen by user
  dependency_edgelist <- dependency_edgelist[weight != 0]
  setnames(dependency_edgelist,
           old=c("src_filepath","dest_filepath"),
           new=c("from","to"))

  # Build directed graph
  file_network <- model_directed_graph(dependency_edgelist,
                                       is_bipartite = FALSE,
                                       color = "#f4dbb5",
                                       aggregate_duplicate = FALSE)

  # Replace node list with the complete set of files from Depends,
  # preserving all files including those with no edges after filtering.
  dependency_nodes <- copy(nodes)
  setnames(dependency_nodes, old="filepath", new="name")
  dependency_nodes$type  <- FALSE
  dependency_nodes$color <- "#f4dbb5"
  file_network[["nodes"]] <- dependency_nodes

  return(file_network)
}
```

## 2. Types of graphs and whether they are directed or undirected

### A. Directed unimodal graphs

One node type, direction matters.

- File-to-file dependencies from Depends and Understand
- Issue-to-issue links like blocks or depends on in Jira

These use:
```r
model_graph(directed = TRUE, node_types = list(file = "#f4dbb5"), ...)
```

Making these undirected would lose information. A depends on B is not the same as B depends on A.

---

### B. Bipartite graphs

Two different node types. The direction here is just used to distinguish the two types. It keeps the API consistent, but does not carry the deeper meaning the way it does in category A.

- Author to file
- Commit to file
- Person to thread, which covers mail, GitHub issues and PRs, and Jira, since they all share the same reply table format and the same transform function `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network`

These use:
```r
model_graph(directed = TRUE, node_types = list(developer = "black", file = "#f4dbb5"), ...)
```

Worth noting that mail does not directly give us a sender-to-receiver graph. What we actually get from the transform is a person-to-thread graph. A person-to-person network would only come from projecting that bipartite graph, not from the raw transform output.

---

### C. Symmetric interaction graphs

Relationships where direction does not mean anything.

- Co-change file networks
- Co-authorship networks
- Jira relates-to links

Jira shows up in both A and C because it has two different kinds of links. Some links have a clear direction, like "A blocks B," which is not the same as "B blocks A", so those belong in A. Other links like "relates to" just mean two issues are connected, and it does not matter which one you start from, so those belong here in C.

These use:
```r
model_graph(directed = FALSE, node_types = list(file = "#f4dbb5"), ...)
```

Storing these as directed graphs is not just a style issue; it actually causes wrong results. If file A and file B are both changed in the same commit, that relationship goes both ways equally. If we store it as directed, then algorithms that care about direction, like shortest path or centrality, will get the wrong answer. It also means tools like DV8 or igraph that expect an undirected matrix for co-change analysis will not work correctly.

So I think adding undirected support is necessary, not optional. My proposal for how to do that is in section 3 below. Does this match your thinking?

---

## 3. How I plan to shape `graph.R`

The current `model_directed_graph` takes care of building nodes from edges, typing bipartite graphs, coloring, handling duplicate edges, and setting the graph class. It works well for the gitlog pipelines, but working with Depends showed two gaps:

1. When `aggregate_duplicate = TRUE`, the edge table gets shrunk down to just `from`, `to`, and `weight`, which throws away any extra columns. For Depend,s that would wipe out all the per-type dependency counts.
2. The node list always gets built from the edge table, so any file that has no edges after filtering quietly disappears.

On top of that, we need undirected support from section 2C. So I want to propose replacing `model_directed_graph` with a single `model_graph` function as the next step.

The proposed signature looks like this:

```r
model_graph <- function(edgelist,
                        directed    = TRUE,
                        node_types,        # named list: type label -> hex color
                        nodes,             # pre-built node table from transform
                        aggregate_duplicate = TRUE)
```

- `directed` handles both directed and undirected graphs in one function. For undirected graphs, the edges get sorted before aggregation, so A-B and B-A count as the same edge.
- `node_types` is a named list that replaces the old `is_bipartite` and `color` parameters. One entry means unimodal, two means bipartite, three or more handles graphs with multiple node types.
- `nodes` is always provided by the transform. The transform is responsible for deriving or normalizing the node table from the parse output before calling `model_graph`. This means `model_graph` never needs to guess which nodes exist from the edgelist alone, and isolated nodes are never silently lost.
- `aggregate_duplicate` works the same as it does now.

`model_directed_graph` would stay as a simple wrapper around `model_graph`, so nothing else in the codebase breaks.

**Does this work for you, and should `model_graph` be part of this issue?**

---

## 4. Parse output structure differences

One thing that came up in the last meeting is worth addressing here. The parse functions across the codebase do not all return data in the same shape. There are four patterns, and each one requires the transform to do different work before reaching `model_graph`:

1. **Single flat event table** - gitlog, R dependencies. One table where everything is combined. The transform derives the edgelist by picking the relevant columns and derives the node table from the unique values in those columns. Both are passed to `model_graph`.
2. **Reply table** - mbox, GitHub, JIRA after recombining. One table is already in a shared format. The transform maps the reply columns to `from` and `to` for the edgelist and derives the node table from those same columns. Both are passed to `model_graph`.
3. **Two tables with wide edgelist** - Depends. The node table already exists from the parse output and is normalized by the transform. The edgelist is copied in full to preserve all dependency type columns, and a canonical `weight` column is computed. Both are passed to `model_graph`.
4. **Two tables with non-standard schema** - Understand. The node and edge tables exist but use different key names and column structures. The transform normalizes both before passing them to `model_graph`.

In all four cases, the transform is responsible for producing a clean `(nodes, edgelist)` pair. By the time `model_graph` is called, the work of shaping and splitting the data is already done. This also means isolated nodes are always preserved for pipelines that have a separate node table, because the transform pulls the node list from the parse output before any edge filtering happens.

The part that still needs fixing is that some transform functions return data under different key names and without a graph class, which makes the output unpredictable for anything downstream. Cleaning that up is included in the proposed next steps below.

---

## 5. Preserving the Depends edge data

Git log data already comes in a clean format with just `from`, `to`, and `weight`. Depends is different because it gives each dependency type its own column, like Call, Import, or Extend, with a count for each file pair.

What I did to handle this:

- Copy the full Depends edge table so no columns get dropped
- Compute a single `weight` column from all dependency types or just the ones the user picks
- Pass the full normalized edgelist and node table to `model_graph` with `aggregate_duplicate = FALSE`

So the final `graph$edgelist` has `from`, `to`, `weight`, and all the original dependency type columns. Nothing gets thrown away. Algorithms use `weight,` and anyone who needs more detail can still get to the individual columns.

---

## 6. Passing extra information through transforms

The pattern I am using is that each transform is in charge of:

- Producing `from`, `to`, and `weight`
- Keeping any extra edge info like churn, timestamps, status, or link type
- Deriving or normalizing the node table from the parse output
- Optionally adding node info like role or label

Then `model_graph` builds the graph and keeps whatever extra columns come through. Not everything has to become `weight`. Weight is just the number that graph algorithms run on. Everything else stays in the graph object and can be used for analysis or visualization.

This should work the same way across other pipelines:

- Git: commit counts, churn, timestamps
- Jira: issue priority, type, link type
- GitHub: review count, PR state
- Understand: dependency category

If something does not fit naturally as an edge or node attribute, it probably should not be pushed into the graph at all.

## Next Steps — Graph Constructor Redesign (from 2/20/26 Capstone Meeting)

---

### 1. Create One Constructor Function Per Graph Type

- Instead of a single unified function, create a separate constructor for each graph type
- Each constructor's core is two lines, following the pattern already in `graph.R` lines 135 and 136:
  ```r
  graph <- list(nodes = nodes, edgelist = edgelist)
  class(graph) <- c("directed_graph", class(graph))
  ```
- New functions follow this same pattern with a different class name assigned on line 136
- Look at igraph for inspiration on how it distinguishes directed vs undirected and bipartite, and follow a similar naming and typing convention

---

### 2. Simplify Constructor Parameters

- Remove `node_types` as a named list and replace with two simple parameters: `label` and `color`
- Place node-related parameters before `edgelist` in the function signature
- Node information belongs in the node table that the transform passes in, not as standalone parameters to the constructor

---

### 3. Keep Constructors as Pure Constructors

- Graph constructors only build the graph and do not group, filter, or normalize data
- The transform function decides which constructor to call based on the pipeline and graph type
- Grouping edges and building the node table stays in the transform layer

---

### 4. Preserve the Existing Output Structure

- All constructors must return a named list with exactly two elements: `nodes` and `edgelist`
- Respect the existing columns in both tables and do not drop columns that downstream functions depend on
- In `transform_dependencies_to_network` specifically, the extra columns from Depends (Import, Call, Use, etc.) must be accounted for, since the graph can ultimately only hold a single weight value per edge

---

### 5. Add Type Verification

- Add input checking to each constructor to verify the input is a recognized graph type
- This protects downstream functions like projections, smells, and exports from receiving the wrong structure

---

### 6. Verify Downstream Compatibility

- Review all functions in `graph.R` that currently depend on `model_directed_graph`
- Run projections (`bipartite_graph_projection`, `temporal_graph_projection`), community detection (`community_oslom`), and social smells against the new constructors to confirm nothing breaks
- Projections must work correctly across all graph types produced by the new constructors

---

### 7. Understand the Graph Constraint

- A graph can only represent a single edge between two nodes, with one number as weight and a direction
- Any richer data, like multiple dependency types between the same two files, must be collapsed in the transform layer before reaching the constructor
- This is the boundary between what the transform does and what the constructor does

## Question: Transform Function Design

When designing the transform layer, should each graph type have its own 
dedicated transform function, or should one transform function per pipeline 
accept a graph type parameter and handle all types internally?

### Option A — One function per graph type (current approach)

Each function has one job and one output type. Adding a new graph type means 
adding a new function.

```r
transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network(project_git)
transform_gitlog_to_heterogeneous_network(project_git)
transform_gitlog_to_temporal_network(project_git)
```

### Option B — One function per pipeline with a type parameter

One entry point per pipeline. The function internally decides which constructor 
to call based on the type parameter.

```r
transform_gitlog_to_network(project_git, type = "bipartite")
transform_gitlog_to_network(project_git, type = "heterogeneous")
transform_gitlog_to_network(project_git, type = "temporal")
```

### Tradeoff

Option A keeps each function small and easy to read but adds more functions 
over time. Option B keeps the interface simpler for the user but puts more 
logic inside one function, which could get large as more graph types are added.

### git.R: New Heterogeneous Transform

A new function, `transform_gitlog_to_heterogeneous_network`, was added to the git pipeline. It combines authors, commits, and files into one heterogeneous graph with three node types and two edge types.

The transform builds the nodes table by making a separate table for each node type and combining them. It builds the edgelist by creating author-to-commit edges with a weight of 1 and commit-to-file edges with a weight equal to the total lines added and removed. Both tables are passed into `model_heterogeneous_graph`, which assigns the class and returns the graph.

This is the first pipeline to use the heterogeneous graph constructor and is meant to serve as a reference for other pipelines when they get updated.

---

### Heterogeneous Graph and Projections

The `model_heterogeneous_graph` constructor is not directly compatible with the existing `bipartite_graph_projection` and `temporal_graph_projection` functions. Those functions filter nodes using a boolean `type` column (`TRUE` or `FALSE`), but the heterogeneous graph uses string labels like `"author"`, `"commit"`, and `"file"` to distinguish node types. Passing a heterogeneous graph into those functions would return zero rows because the filter `type == TRUE` or `type == FALSE` would never match a string. A second issue is that the heterogeneous edgelist mixes multiple edge types in one table, while the projection functions expect a single bipartite structure where `from` always refers to one node type and `to` always refers to the other.

Two paths forward are under consideration: 

The first is to add an extractor function that slices a heterogeneous graph into a proper `bipartite_graph` before the projection step. The extractor would filter nodes and edges by a chosen type pair and recode the string type to `TRUE`/`FALSE` to match what the projection functions expect. No existing code would need to change.

The second path is to use R S3 dispatch to convert `bipartite_graph_projection` into a generic function with separate methods for `bipartite_graph` and `heterogeneous_graph`. The `bipartite_graph` method would keep the current `TRUE`/`FALSE` behavior, and the `heterogeneous_graph` method would accept a string mode like `"file"` or `"author"` directly. This is a cleaner long-term design, but requires restructuring the existing projection functions.

The extractor approach would be the easier approach in the short term, but the S3 dispatch approach would be the target design if projections on heterogeneous graphs become a common part of the pipeline.
